contributions.title: The authors present fastText as a simple, efficient text classification baseline that combines a rank-constrained linear model with fast loss computation to scale to large corpora and output spaces.
contributions.description: The authors present fastText as a simple, efficient text classification baseline that combines a rank-constrained linear model with fast loss computation to scale to large corpora and output spaces.

contributions.title: The authors present a simple text-classification baseline whose word features can be averaged into useful sentence representations, achieving performance comparable to recent deep-learning-inspired methods on several tasks with substantially lower computational cost.
contributions.description: The authors present a simple text-classification baseline whose word features can be averaged into useful sentence representations, achieving performance comparable to recent deep-learning-inspired methods on several tasks with substantially lower computational cost.

claims.statement: fastText uses a rank-constrained linear model in which a lookup matrix maps words to representations that are averaged into a text representation and passed to a linear classifier.
The model computes class probabilities with softmax and trains by minimizing negative log-likelihood over document labels.
Documents are represented as normalized bags of features, and training uses asynchronous stochastic gradient descent on multiple CPUs with a linearly decaying learning rate.

Using hierarchical softmax based on a Huffman coding tree reduces the stated training complexity from O(kh) to O(h log₂(k)), where k is the number of classes and h is the text representation dimension.
At prediction time, depth-first search tracks the maximum leaf probability and prunes low-probability branches because a node's probability cannot exceed its parent's probability.
The authors report observing O(h log₂(k)) prediction complexity in practice and describe extending the search to retrieve the top T targets using a binary heap at a stated cost of O(log(T)).
The authors report that fastText often matches deep learning classifiers in accuracy while being many orders of magnitude faster for training and evaluation.
The authors conclude that fastText achieves performance on par with recently proposed deep-learning-inspired methods on several tasks while being much faster.
The authors report training fastText on more than one billion words in less than ten minutes using a standard multicore CPU.
The authors report classifying half a million sentences among 312,000 classes in less than one minute.
fastText supplements bag-of-words features with bag-of-n-gram features to capture partial information about local word order.
The implementation hashes n-grams using the hash function cited to Mikolov et al. (2011), with 10 million bins for bigrams alone and 100 million bins otherwise.
The authors report that their tailored implementation is at least 2–5 times faster in practice than an implementation using Vowpal Wabbit with the options --nn, --ngrams, and --log multi.

In the main classification experiments, fastText uses 10 hidden units and five epochs, with a learning rate selected on validation data from {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5}; the evaluation follows the eight datasets and protocol of Zhang et al. (2015).
The authors report that adding bigrams improves classification performance by 1–4%, with overall accuracy slightly better than char-CNN and char-CRNN and slightly worse than VDCNN.
The authors report that adding trigrams raises Sogou accuracy to 97.1%.

The extracted accuracy table reports fastText with 10 hidden units and bigrams achieving 92.5, 96.8, 98.6, 95.7, 63.9, 72.3, 60.2, and 94.6 percent test accuracy for AG, Sogou, DBP, Yelp P., Yelp F., Yah. A., Amz. F., and Amz. P., respectively; these column assignments remain unverified.

Under Tang et al.'s evaluation protocol, the authors describe fastText as competitive, report that n-grams up to length five perform best on validation data, and suggest that the absence of pretrained word embeddings may explain an accuracy difference of about one percentage point.

The extracted Tang et al. comparison reports fastText test accuracies of 64.2, 66.2, 66.6, and 45.2 percent on Yelp’13, Yelp’14, Yelp’15, and IMDB, compared with LSTM-GRNN values of 65.1, 67.1, 67.6, and 45.3 percent; the table alignment remains unverified.

The authors report training fastText in less than a minute on the classification datasets using a CPU with 20 threads, while character CNN and VDCNN methods trained on an NVIDIA Tesla K40 GPU are several orders of magnitude slower; they acknowledge that newer CUDA convolution implementations could speed up char-CNN by a factor of ten.

The extracted training-time table assigns fastText with 10 hidden units and bigrams single-epoch times of 1, 7, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, and 10 seconds to AG, Sogou, DBpedia, Yelp P., Yelp F., Yah. A., Amz. F., and Amz. P., respectively; these column assignments remain unverified.
The method combines a rank-constrained linear model with fast loss computation.

The scalability evaluation predicts tags from YFCC100M titles and captions without using images. After removing words and tags occurring fewer than 100 times, the task contains 91,188,648 training examples with 1.5 billion tokens, 930,497 validation examples, 543,424 test examples, 297,141 vocabulary words, and 312,116 tags; evaluation uses precision at one.

The tag-prediction experiments run fastText for five epochs and compare hidden-layer sizes of 50 and 200 against a most-frequent-tag baseline and linear Tagspace; training uses 20 threads for both models, and test timing uses one thread.
The authors report similar tag-prediction performance for fastText and Tagspace with a small hidden layer, and a substantial accuracy improvement from adding bigrams to fastText.

The authors attribute fastText's inference advantage in the space of more than 300,000 tags to its fast inference procedure, contrasting it with Tagspace's computation of scores for every class; they report obtaining a better-quality model more than an order of magnitude faster and a 600-fold test-phase speedup.

The extracted tag-prediction table reports precision at one of 2.2 for the frequency baseline; 30.1 and 35.6 for Tagspace with 50 and 200 hidden units; and 31.2, 36.7, 41.1, and 46.1 for fastText with 50 units, 50 units plus bigrams, 200 units, and 200 units plus bigrams, respectively. These table associations remain unverified.

Under the extracted training/test column order, fastText with 200 hidden units and bigrams takes 13 minutes 38 seconds to train and 1 minute 37 seconds to test, compared with 5 hours 32 minutes and 15 hours for Tagspace with 200 units. These column associations remain unverified.
The authors state that fastText's word features can be averaged to form good sentence representations, contrasting them with unsupervised word2vec vectors.
The authors report that the speedup over neural-network-based methods increases with dataset size and reaches at least 15,000-fold.
